source.title: MOON Embedding: Multimodal Representation Learning for E-commerce Search Advertising
source.authors: Chenghan Fu; Daoze Zhang; Yukang Lin; Zhanheng Nie; Xiang Zhang; Jianyu Liu; Yueran Liu; Wanxian Guan; Pengjie Wang; Jian Xu; Bo Zheng

record.file_problem: No apparent file problem; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study explores scaling behavior in multimodal e-commerce representation learning, a new setting, using retrieval recall rather than language-model held-out cross-entropy.
record.gate_note: The study reports scaling results for training-image count, tokens per image, and negative-sample count, plus a downstream user-behavior-sequence result. It does not report results for language-model held-out loss, model-parameter or compute sweeps, compute-optimal allocation, or downstream scaling as a function of pretraining loss. Values used only to select the base model are not included as rows.
record.test_reason: The study reports its own scaling sweeps in a new setting: contrastive post-training of a 4B multimodal model for e-commerce retrieval. It varies training-image count and tokens per image, so its results bear on V5 (scaling in fine-tuning and other modalities). The measure is image-search recall, not held-out loss, and the sweeps are shown only as unlabelled-value figures with no power-law fit. The evidence is therefore weak.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors say scaling in e-commerce search shows clear diminishing marginal returns. They claim that token count and recall follow a scaling law with diminishing returns, and that recall trends upward with more negatives before plateauing at 40K–80K. They also report that longer behaviour sequences raise the exchange rate. They fit no power law and do not study parameter scaling.
record.recipe_differences: This is a multimodal e-commerce representation-learning study using image-based search recall and downstream exchange rate, not a language-model held-out cross-entropy scaling experiment. It does not fit the original studies' parameter, token, or compute loss laws.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported trends vary with the scale factor: image count and tokens per image show diminishing marginal gains, negative samples show no further recall improvement from 40K to 80K, and the exchange rate rises as behavior-sequence length increases from 100 to 3000.

fits_no_version.finding: Image-search recall rises overall with negative-sample pool size but does not improve from 40K to 80K negatives.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In contrastive multimodal retrieval training, recall gains from enlarging the negative pool saturate.

fits_no_version.finding: The exchange rate between recall gains and CTR AUC gains rises from 0.0 to 1.0 as behaviour-sequence length grows from 100 to 3000.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Longer user behaviour sequences increase how much intermediate-metric gains translate into downstream CTR AUC.

record.problems: The scaling plots provide no tabulated values or uncertainty estimates. The study fixes the base model at TBStars-VL-4B and explicitly does not examine parameter scaling; it does not report power-law fits or exponents.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant reported scaling result omitted.

untested.parts: No held-out LM loss or parameter, token or compute sweeps. Parameter scaling is explicitly excluded.
No shape comparison at fixed parameter count.
No loss measure and no power-law fit or exponents. The power-law form itself is untested; only the monotone diminishing-returns trend in recall is shown. No video, repeated-data or transfer tests.

No downstream performance against model scale or pretraining loss. Section 5.3 lists scale increases across versions but reports no per-version metric, and those increases are confounded with architecture and data changes.

record.verdict_notes: No label is given for V5. The linked rows show only a monotone, decelerating rise in recall, from figures without values or fits. This neither establishes nor contradicts a power-law form, and the reader's limits_scope label rested on untested parts, which the rules exclude. Section 5.3's version-to-version scale-ups (0.2B→4B parameters, 230B→2400B tokens) come with no per-version metrics and are confounded with other changes, so they are not rows.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out language-model pretraining loss or parameter, token, or compute power-law tests.
No small-run fits or predictions of substantially larger runs.
No fixed-compute allocation sweep or comparison of optimal parameter and token growth.
No architecture-shape comparison at fixed parameter count.

Tests multimodal e-commerce retrieval recall as training-image count and tokens per image vary. It does not test held-out loss, establish that the curves have the same power-law form as text pretraining, fit exponents, or test video, repeated-data, transfer, or other modalities and regimes.
No scaling analysis of downstream task performance against model scale or pretraining loss.
No comparison of fitting choices or exponents, compute-optimal splits, or evidence that the tested token curves depart from a fitted power law.

rows.subject: TBStars-VL-4B
rows.operation_detail: Varied the number of training images.
rows.value: figure only; text states recall increases as the number of training images grows, with marginal gains tapering off
rows.note: The paper does not provide numerical curve values or fit a power law for this sweep.
rows.check: Recall rises monotonically with diminishing returns, but there are no axis values (x only as % of 300M images) and no fit. Whether the curve has a power-law form, as V5 requires, can't be read. The measure is downstream recall, not loss.

rows.subject: TBStars-VL-4B
rows.operation_detail: Varied the number of tokens per image.
rows.value: figure only; text states recall improves as tokens per image increase, with the rate of improvement gradually declining
rows.note: The paper describes diminishing marginal gains but gives no numerical curve values or power-law fit.
rows.check: Same as R1: the figure only shows recall improving with a declining rate as tokens per image grow. No values, no fit, and recall rather than loss.

rows.subject: MOON
rows.operation_detail: Varied the number of negative samples used in contrastive training.
rows.value: No recall improvement when increasing from 40K to 80K negative samples
rows.note: The study says recall trends upward as negative samples increase overall, but specifically reports no improvement from 40K to 80K.
rows.check: The link is correct. Note the text reports an overall upward trend that plateaus between 40K and 80K negatives; the absent state applies only to that last step. Negative-pool size is not a parameter, token or compute factor.

rows.subject: MOON
rows.operation_detail: Varied the length of user behavior sequences.
rows.note: The exchange rate is defined as downstream AUC change divided by intermediate-metric change; this is a downstream sequence-length result, not a pretraining-loss scaling result.
rows.check: The link is correct. The exchange rate (ΔAUC/Δrecall) against behaviour-sequence length is not a loss or scale law in any version's sense.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Multimodal e-commerce retrieval with TBStars-VL-4B, varying training-image count or tokens per image
reader_labels.reason: Recall rises with diminishing marginal gains, but the study does not fit or establish the claimed power-law form; the reported measure and setting are limited to retrieval recall in e-commerce. Rows R1 and R2.
